Day 74 of 100 · Kubernetes

Kubernetes Deployments

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityKubernetesPublished artifact recovered

Deployments sit above ReplicaSets to manage stateless application rollouts declaratively, including replacement strategy and revision history.

Architecture / mental model

Deployment → ReplicaSet revision(s) → Pods

How it works

A Deployment declares replicas, a selector, a Pod template and an update strategy. Kubernetes creates and manages ReplicaSets underneath it to move the workload toward the requested revision.

When `spec.template` changes, a Deployment can create a new ReplicaSet, scale it up and scale the old one down according to the rollout strategy instead of replacing every Pod manually.

The project lab keeps the manifest in the Kubernetes repository so rollout behavior is evidence in source control rather than a console action nobody can reproduce.

Hands-on reference

kubectl apply -f day-74-deployments/deployment.yaml
kubectl get deployments
kubectl get rs
kubectl get pods -l app=web
kubectl rollout status deployment/web
kubectl rollout history deployment/web

Verification

Apply the Deployment, change the container image in the Pod template and apply again. Watch the new ReplicaSet and Pods appear while the old ReplicaSet scales down, then inspect rollout status/history.

Field note / gotcha

Changing fields outside `spec.template` does not necessarily create a new Pod-template revision. Know which part of the object drives rollout behavior.

Security considerations

Deployments repeat the Pod security context and image configuration across replicas, so unsafe defaults become fleet-wide. Pin trusted images and keep service-account/privilege settings explicit.

What I learned

ReplicaSets are the replica mechanics; Deployments add the release-management layer most stateless applications actually need.
